nodes.question: When does exchanging a limit with an operation give a wrong answer?
nodes.why: Pointwise convergence alone does not permit interchange of integration and limit.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Pointwise convergence uses input-dependent thresholds, while uniform convergence controls every point simultaneously. Integration, differentiation and summation require suitable convergence hypotheses; Rudin gives explicit contrary examples.

nodes.question: Which collections can consistently be assigned size or probability?
nodes.why: A definable collection does not automatically possess a countably additive measure.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Sigma-algebras encode permitted measurable events; countably additive measures assign size. Lebesgue's theory includes non-measurable set counterexamples showing a boundary to unrestricted intuitive volume.

nodes.question: What happens if we treat functions themselves as points?
nodes.why: Pointwise function equality is not the same as equality almost everywhere; weak convergence does not imply norm convergence.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Lp norms and Hilbert inner products give geometry to function classes; weak and strong convergence describe distinct observational limits. Functions differing almost everywhere may represent one Lp element.

nodes.question: Why are infinite-dimensional transformations not just enormous matrices?
nodes.why: An operator may not be defined on all inputs; boundedness, dense domains and self-adjointness are substantive.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Hahn–Banach and bounded/closed graph theorems analyze linear functionals and operators. Unbounded operators have domains and spectra whose analysis requires more than finite-dimensional eigenvector intuition.

nodes.question: When does repeated iteration certify that a unique solution exists?
nodes.why: Continuous maps need not contract or have uniquely attracting fixed points.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Banach's contraction theorem couples a complete metric space with an invariant contraction to guarantee a unique fixed point and convergent iteration.

nodes.question: Why is complex differentiability so restrictive?
nodes.why: A function can be real differentiable in two variables but not holomorphic.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Holomorphicity links the Cauchy–Riemann equations, contour integrals and analytic rigidity; Cauchy's formula recovers interior values from boundary data.

nodes.question: How can a contour around singularities compute a difficult real integral?
nodes.why: The residue theorem does not justify an arbitrary real-to-complex contour with poles on its boundary.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Laurent coefficients and residues turn closed-contour integrals into local singular contributions, subject to decay, branch and region assumptions.
